title: Seventeen Years After This Painting, Its Maker Was Commanding a Concentration Camp
standfirst: Sever Burada painted *Anemone* in his last year on a state-funded scholarship in Paris. Seventeen years later he commanded Vapniarka, a Romanian-run camp in Transnistria, through the worst weeks of a poisoning epidemic that left prisoners paralysed for life. In 2021 a Bucharest project nearly listed him alongside communism's own victims.

sections.heading: Little Stars and Flowers Around a War Criminal's Portrait
sections.body: In 2021 a Bucharest project called *Artists in Communist Prisons* — run by the critic Cosmin Năsui through the city's PostModernism Museum, drawing on files held by Romania's archive of former secret-police records — put up a page naming fifty-five artists it framed as victims of the postwar communist regime. Four of the fifty-five got special treatment: portraits ringed with little stars and flowers, the decoration reserved for the set's martyrs. One of the four was Sever Burada. The researcher Olga Ștefan, who had read most of the surviving prisoner memoirs from a Transnistrian camp called [Vapniarka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vapniarka_concentration_camp) for her own doctoral thesis, recognised the name and [objected in print](https://platzforma.md/arhive/390467): the page said Burada had been convicted only for "legionary activity" — membership in the wartime far right, the same low-grade charge that put plenty of genuine political prisoners away. He had not. Năsui's own project later traced the confusion to two earlier books on Burada, a 1997 exhibition catalogue and a 2010 biography, that had misled his researchers before they reached the archival file itself. That file gave the actual charge: Burada was convicted for "applying bestial treatment to political prisoners." Năsui took the profile down. Ștefan has argued that quietly removing a name is not the same as correcting what put it there in the first place.

sections.heading: A Drawing Teacher Signs a Sketch From a Bulgarian Prison Camp
sections.body: Burada was born Sever Burădescu on 14 January 1896 in Craiova, into an Aromanian family; his parents were Petre Burădescu and Ștefana, his siblings Traian and Cornelia. He studied at Craiova's Carol I high school under the painter Ioan Stăncescu Giovanni and the sculptor Ion Dumitriu-Bârlad, then at the School of Fine Arts in Bucharest from 1915 to 1919 under George Demetrescu Mirea and Jean Alexandru Steriadi. Somewhere inside those same enrolment years the record also places him at the front and then in captivity: a drawing signed and dated "13.I.917 Hascovo Severo Burădescu" — a fellow prisoner's head, worked in blue coloured pencil and cross-hatching — survives in the Craiova Art Museum, made inside the prisoner-of-war camp at Haskovo, Bulgaria. How a student who shows up continuously enrolled at a Bucharest academy also ended up captured and interned abroad is not something any source reconciles; the record simply holds both facts side by side.

sections.heading: First Prize in a Competition Named for a Painter He Never Studied Under
sections.body: Burada graduated in 1919 and won outright first place in the competition for the Nicolae Grigorescu scholarship, which paid for five further years of study in Paris. At the École des Beaux-Arts he trained under François Flameng, Émile Bernard, Ferdinand Cormon and Lucien Simon, showed at the Salon of French Artists from 1922 to 1925, and had a work bought by the French state off the 1923 Interallied Exhibition. *Anemone* belongs to the tail of that Paris decade, one of a run of flower studies and portraits made in the years just before he returned to Romania in 1926. Wikidata and the Romanian record file his work as postimpressionism; the entry attached to this feature calls the same painting Impressionism. Neither label gets much scrutiny in what little is written about him — the record is far more interested in what he did after Paris than in what he painted there.

sections.heading: A Painting Colony on a Coast Romania Would Later Lose
sections.body: Back in Romania after 1926, Burada joined what's now called the Balchik School — Romanian avant-garde painters drawn during the interwar years to the Black Sea town of Balchik, then part of Romania's Southern Dobruja until the [Treaty of Craiova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balchik) returned it to Bulgaria in 1940, whose houses and Turkish inhabitants filled the group's canvases. Around that anchor sits a comfortable, well-reviewed interwar career: membership in the Tinerimea artistică society, solo shows in Craiova and Bucharest between 1924 and 1937, and work later held by the Cotroceni museum, the Constanța Art Museum, the Nicolae Iorga Memorial Museum and the Șuțu Palace, alongside a run of Balchik canvases — *Balchik Noon*, *Balchik Gulf*, *Tatar Houses in Balchik*, *Balchik Hills*. It is the record of a working painter who had already banked his prizes and kept exhibiting steadily for a decade. Nothing in it anticipates what came next.

sections.heading: Commandant Through the Worst Weeks of a Poisoning
sections.body: Burada re-enlisted for the Second World War as a reserve captain. "A drawing teacher in civilian life," one survivor account records, "the reserve captain Burădescu was the sadistic type, cruel and refined"; his brutal conduct toward internees, the same account adds, was fed by a deep-rooted hatred of Jews. He took command of Vapniarka, a Romanian-run camp in occupied Transnistria holding roughly 1,200 Jewish and political prisoners, after Ion Murgescu, sometime around the end of 1942, and was replaced by Hristache Popovici that February. His tenure therefore spans the camp's worst stretch: from late 1942 Romanian authorities had been feeding prisoners *Lathyrus sativus* — grass pea, ordinarily animal fodder, carrying a neurotoxin — and by January 1943 hundreds were showing the stiffness and weakness of lathyrism; camp doctors led by Arthur Kessler eventually counted 117 prisoners left permanently paralysed. No source says Burada ordered the rations himself. They do record what he told Kessler when pressed on why prisoners kept dying: "How do you know we want to keep you alive?" A hunger strike finally forced the toxic ration's end in late January 1943; the following month Popovici took over and restored bread and family parcels.

sections.heading: Convicted in 1945, Not Locked Up Until the 1950s
sections.body: Burada was tried and convicted as a war criminal in 1945, the charge on his file reading, in the original, the application of "bestial treatment to political prisoners." His family petitioned King Michael for clemency that June. What happened between verdict and sentence is one of the gaps this record doesn't close: by one account he was not actually arrested until the 1950s, under a different regime from the one that had convicted him, and was released on 28 January 1960. He went back to painting, though nothing from those years matches what had won him the Grigorescu prize four decades earlier. He died in Bucharest in September 1968. Compare his file to that of Sabin Motora, the last of Vapniarka's commandants, who defied orders to march the camp's remaining prisoners toward German control and was recognised by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations in 1983. Two men ran the same camp within months of each other in 1943. One is remembered for saving prisoners. The other very nearly got a place, ringed in stars and flowers, among communism's own victims.
